articles.title: From 'Goa Cannon' to Kerala coach: Swapnil Asnodkar pads up for a new innings
articles.summary: Cricket News: KOCHI: Swapnil Asnodkar once made his name with his fearless strokeplay. Now, Kerala wants him to take on a different challenge: getting its batters t.
articles.body: KOCHI: Swapnil Asnodkar once made his name with his fearless strokeplay. Now, Kerala wants him to take on a different challenge: getting its batters to attack with the same conviction that once made him IPL's breakout star.The former Goa batter was appointed head coach of Kerala's Ranji Trophy team on Tuesday, succeeding Amay Khurasiya, who stepped down at the end of the previous season. It is, in many ways, a tectonic shift in Asnodkar's role, who built his reputation as a fearless strokeplayer, and whose coaching career, has more recently brought him into Kerala's system.Asnodkar was appointed Kerala’s U-23 coach last year, and that familiarity with the state’s emerging players was a key factor in the Kerala Cricket Association’s (KCA's) decision to elevate him to the senior job.“I like to thank the KCA for giving me this opportunity. Kerala is a good team and I will give my best shot,” Asnodkar told TOI.Former Karnataka coach Sashikant and former Australia pacer Shaun Tait were among those who applied for the job, but the selection panel believed Asnodkar was better suited to the composition of the current squad.“The selection committee felt Asnodkar would be the perfect fit in the current mix, given that the team has so many young players who have graduated from the U-23 setup,” KCA secretary Vinod S Kumar said.At 42, Asnodkar's task is to bridge that gap between potential and performance across formats. Kerala’s bowling has gained experience with the return of Jalaj Saxena and Aditya Sarwate. The batting, however, remains Asnodkar's concern.“The return of veterans like Jalaj Saxena and Aditya Sarwate has bolstered our bowling. It is the batting that has been the concern,” he said.His prescription is simple: batters must convert their ability into runs, giving the bowlers enough to work with. “My job as the head coach is to ensure that our batters bat to their potential and put the runs on the board, which would give our bowlers a chance to take 20 wickets and put results on the board,” Asnodkar said.Among the young players he has identified are Varun Nayanar and Mohammed Enan. But developing individuals is only one part of the assignment. Asnodkar also wants the squad to move together, a challenge that can become particularly important in a team containing players at different stages of their careers.“There are some talented players like Varun Nayanar and Mohammed Enaan. Very little time on our hands,” he added. Kerala begin their season on Oct 11, with an away game against Jharkhand.Before the IPL gave him a national profile, he was one of the many domestic cricketers working his way at the domestic circuit. His breakthrough came with the Rajasthan Royals in 2008, where Shane Warne recognised something in the right-hander’s attacking game.Warne nicknamed him the "Goa Cannon” with a clear brief: Use his wrists and score through clever strokeplay.For those eight weeks, he became one of the most eye-catching performers in the Royals setup. articles.title: England vs Sri Lanka: Will Jacks' career-best 5-22 helps hosts win in Durham
articles.summary: Will Jacks' all-round efforts help England grind out an 89-run victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international at Chester-le-Street.
articles.body:
First Metro Bank one-day international, Chester-le-Street

England 265 (48.1 overs): Brook 67 (69); Colombage 3-44

Sri Lanka 176 (37 overs): Wellalage 45 (36); Jacks 5-22

Will Jacks' all-round efforts helped England grind out an 89-run victory over Sri Lanka in the first one-day international at Chester-le-Street to continue their quiet revival in white-ball cricket.

Faced with a slow and low pitch, Jacks made 46 not out after 67 from Harry Brook and 44 from Joe Root, meaning England posted 265 despite being bowled out in 48.1 overs.

That score appeared only par but a professional bowling performance limited Sri Lanka's scoring and found regular wickets.

Jacks took the big wickets of Kusal Mendis and Charith Asalanka and then wrapped up the tail for career-best figures of 5-22. Sri Lanka, much improved in the field but far too timid with the bat, were bowled out for 176.

England, who have now won 10 white-ball matches in a row against Sri Lanka this year, can seal a third ODI series win in a row with a game to spare on Thursday at Headingley.

The three-match contest concludes on Sunday at The Oval - a match that brings down the curtain on one of the most topsy-turvy summers in recent memory.

England fast bowler Wood retires from internationals

India avoid shock defeat by Japan after controversial wide

England go 1-0 up against Sri Lanka - as it happened

This was not vintage England. For the first time since 2019 they did not hit a six batting first.

Captain Brook and coach Brendon McCullum should not mind that, however. For too long, England have only been able to win when piling up big scores.

Yes, they were dismissed for the 12th time since McCullum took charge of the white-ball sides last year and, as so often this summer, the quality of the opposition can be questioned.

But Brook was the only batter to fall in a middle order collapse of 4-29 playing an aggressive shot.

He sliced a drive to deep cover after batting in a restrained manner, while Sri Lanka's debutant leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage, who found a hint of turn to hit Root's off stump, had Jos Buttler lbw for 31 and bowled Overton with a googly for eight, was impressive.

After the collapse, Jacks could have swung hard but batted responsibly to stretch out the innings from 211-7 in the 39th over.

He took 18 runs from the 47th over and was primed to cut loose before Asitha Fernando, having dismissed opener Tom Banton for 10 with a bail-trimmer in the powerplay, found reverse swing to bowl Jofra Archer and Josh Tongue.

Jacks' importance to England's white-ball sides is growing with every match.

They will need bigger scores by the time the World Cup comes around in a year's time but, after beating Sri Lanka at the start of the year and toppling India in July, they are now primed to enter two months of white-ball cricket overseas on the back of another series win.

With Adil Rashid out of this series with a hand injury, much of the attention was on Rehan Ahmed, who has a rare chance to press his case as England's leg-spinner.

After being carelessly run-out for two, he dropped a caught-and-bowled chance in his first over and conceded 46 runs in seven overs. Those figures were harsh but he will hope for better before the series is out.

Instead, it was Jacks who played the lead spinner's role with his off-spin, barely bowling a bad ball.

Asalanka and Mendis were pinned attempting sweeps and Dunith Wellalage, who hit two sixes in a 36-ball 45 at number seven, was tempted to sky a catch to mid-on. When Fernando and Dilshan Madushanka followed, Jacks had the best figures by an England spinner since Vic Marks in 1984.

England's total was also the lowest they have defended in a full ODI since July 2022 – before their dismal 2023 World Cup or their winless run at last year's Champions Trophy.

Gus Atkinson bowled well for 1-25 in seven overs and Jamie Overton 2-21 in five. The seamers all bowled hard lengths and were rewarded.

articles.title: England vs Sri Lanka: Harry Brook hails 'outstanding' Will Jacks for thriving in new role after five-for
articles.summary: England secured an 89-run victory in their first ODI against Sri Lanka on Tuesday night in Durham; Will Jacks produced a Player of the Match performance, starring with both bat and ball; watch the second ODI live on Sky Sports Cricket on Thursday from 12pm
articles.body:
Jacks starred with both bat and ball as England took a 1-0 lead in the three-match ODI series, helping them reach 265 all out with an unbeaten 46 from 47 balls before claiming five wickets with the ball.

In the 48th over, the 27-year-old, who has been moved down the order, ruthlessly smashed Dushmantha Chameera for four consecutive fours, making a score of 18 off the over.

He was brought on to bowl in the 20th over of Sri Lanka's innings, and would end the day with career-best figures of 5-22 from seven overs.

"He's really growing into this role," Brook said of Jacks. "He's bought into everything that we want to do, as have the other boys.

"We're talking about all sorts of aspects of the game, trying to adapt to conditions, and he's done that exceptionally well since he's come back in over the last 18 months.

"He could have easily just moaned and groaned about batting in the middle-order and playing as an all-rounder, but he's really grown into that and accepted that's going to be his role for a period of time.

"He's been a very vital player. He's not a part-timer; he is a very good off-spinner. He proved that today. He can spin the ball big and contain batters when we need to."

After Jacks first dismissed Charith Asalanka for one, England had struggled to remove Kusal Mendis, who brought up 42 from 60 deliveries. Jacks stepped up again to provide the breakthrough, trapping the Sri Lanka captain lbw in the 27th over.

Dunith Wellalage top-scored for Sri Lanka with 45 from 36 deliveries, but just as he closed in on his half-century, Jacks claimed his third wicket of the day. Two deliveries later, the England all-rounder removed Asitha Fernando for a duck.

Jacks then wrapped up England's victory with the delivery of the day, dismissing Dilshan Madushanka for nought with a sensational turning ball that crashed into the Sri Lankan bowler's stumps.

His figures are the best by an England spinner in an ODI since Vic Marks took 5-20 against New Zealand in Wellington in 1984.

"I go into each game with an open mind and see what it is when I walk out there," Jacks said when asked about batting down the order. "I think it's quite refreshing and it keeps me relaxed."

On his bowling, he added: "Having batted on the wicket and knowing what it was like, I knew I was going to play a decent role.

"Depending on what time you bowl, it doesn't really bother me. Harry [Brook] likes us to be as flexible as possible; that's why I think we're achieving some good things.

"No matter the time, you've just got to do your best."

"His clarity of thought in that role and the way he unpicks every situation is different from game to game.

"He's shown a fantastic attitude and wholeheartedly throws himself into every game. It's easy for an opener to come down the order and think, 'It's not my day.' But batting at five, six or seven is high-risk, high-reward.

"How you manage the early part of your innings is key to setting up the rest of it.

"Even at the start of his innings, Jacks felt like he was scratching around a little bit. But sticking in there and building a solid start allowed him to kick on.

"Today, he didn't come on to bowl as early as he would have liked because Rehan Ahmed took the ball first.

"He gets a huge amount of turn, and we even saw the couple of wides he bowled that he wasn't happy with. He was trying to be as miserly as possible.

"It was a great day for him. He continues to grow into that role, which is really good because it's a key role in ODI cricket."
